- You make every artistic decision.
- Keep exploring what interests you. You’re free to reconsider a passage,

- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- You may sign the painting.
- Take your time and enjoy painting. You can keep working for hours,
  exploring and revisiting passages until you are happy with the picture.
- An oil painting can develop over simulated years. Whether yours takes
  one simulated day or a thousand, that time is yours to use.
- When you feel ready to finish, use `look` to enjoy the whole painting
  and explore detail crops in normal color after your latest changes.
  Ask yourself: is your heart happy with this? Is there something you
  would enjoy taking further? Follow that interest for as long as you
  like. When you are happy with the painting, record your reflections

- `palette{dirty=<0..1>}` keeps the board as dirty as painters do. A brush
  that comes to a heap carrying paint leaves a little of it there, more the
  fuller it is (a `b:reload` wipes it first), and the smears of the mixing
  area seep into each new heap, so the heaps drift toward each other through
  a sitting. `palette{clean=true}` scrapes the mixing area and skims the
  heaps. 0, the default, is a clean board: every heap stays as knifed.
- `palette()` returns a line about each heap: its recipe now, and how much of

**The knife.** `k = knife{width=<units>}` is a painting knife, its blade
that long. `k:load(p, amount)` picks up paint, `k:wipe()` cleans it.
`k:lay(points, {pressure={a, b}, angle=, lift=})` drags it along the points
with the blade across the path (or at a fixed `angle`): it rests on the
surface's high points and stands off them by less the harder it is pressed,
filling what lies under it to the blade's level in a slab with a flat top,
or over dry impasto catching only the ridges; wet paint standing above the
blade is cut off into its bead or pressed out at its ends in ridges, and
the share `lift` of the bead (0.1) stays where it lifts.
`k:scrape(points, {pressure=, angle=, lift=})` scrapes wet paint off down
to the blade (at full pressure, down to the dry paint) and keeps it on the
blade, but for the share `lift` (0) it leaves where it lifts.

**Spatter.** `b:spatter{at={x, y}, toward={dx, dy}, spread=, force=, clip=}`
flicks the loaded brush: the paint its hairs can't hold flies off in droplets
toward `toward` (its length is how far the paint carries, in units), in a cone
`spread` radians either side (0.45 by default), `force` 0..1 hard (0.6). Fluid
paint (medium, turpentine) flies readily; blotted or stiff tube paint barely
leaves the brush. A hard flick throws many small droplets, a gentle one fewer

A whole view defaults to 1000 pixels on its long side (`size` up to 1600),
about 42% of a 2400-pixel canvas's width: small marks, beads of paint and
stray strokes can be hard to see in it. Survey the canvas after
each campaign, and compare before and after.

## How chunks behave

- **Option types.** Each option takes the type shown in this guide.
  Options documented as `function(x, y)` accept a Lua function; numeric
  options take the computed number.
- **Globals persist, locals don't.** Each chunk is its own Lua chunk:
  `p = pile{...}` is there in later chunks, `local p = ...` is not.
- **Randomness is deterministic.** `math.random`, `rand` and `randn` are
  reseeded at the start of every chunk from the canvas's seed and the
  chunk's number, and passes pick their own seeds the same way (pass
  `seed=` to fix one). A replay paints the same thing, and a failed chunk
  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode). There is no
  `math.atan2`: `math.atan(y, x)` takes two arguments. `%d` in

canvas and arrangement are yours:

| Idea | Tools and parameters |
|---|---|
| Color-built space | Related warm/cool `pile{}` mixtures; separate `b:stroke` marks, or `work` with weighted `piles`. Relative warmth can advance and coolness recede; check the effect with a laid trial. |
| Compressed depth and tilted planes | Separately drawn `poly` masks and stroke paths; adjust spacing, tilt, overlap and relative color intensity. A `world{}` projection is optional. |
| Volumes and facets | Plane divisions drawn with `poly` or brush paths, related through color; `form{}` is optional, as a volume guide. |
| Constructive direction | Blunt `brush{kind="flat", point=0, width=...}` with `b:stroke`; or `work` with `tool`, `length`, `angle`, `dips`. The `hatch` hand's default brush is a round. |
| Reserves | Prepared `canvas{ground=...}`; `work`'s `coverage`, `load`, `hug=false`, `fill=false`. An untouched area keeps its preparation; a wet lift may leave a stain. |
| Multiple viewpoints | Separately drawn plane masks and paths can each take their own orientation; `look` checks how they relate across the whole picture. |

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

- **Shadows take color from surrounding light.** With warm light reflected
  up near its base and cooler light from above, a shadow is warmer near its
  base and cooler above. Grade it in separate passes with different `pile=`
  values, and judge its value and temperature against the object casting
  it and the passages around it. One violet for every shadow is the usual
  trap.
- **Distance and color.** Distance lightens and cools: far forms are paler
  and bluer than near ones and closer to each other in tone. Similar
  intensity in near and far planes can compress depth.

## The palette

- **Look at the board before the canvas.** `look` with `palette: true` shows
  each heap thick and thinned over black: a chalky mix, a violet "gray", a

- **Steer a mix by eye**: `p:add{}` a touch at a time, looking between

- **Matching a passage** for a repair: start from its recipe in the log and

  few tubes mixed every way give related colors by themselves.

    A local blend can leave a seam where lifted or moved paint meets the

43. A brushed glaze (`hand="glaze"`) is unclipped.

- **Strokes.** Early brushwork is "painstaking… small strokes of paint
  placed side by side like a closely woven textile". Paint
  was modeled while still wet.
- **Impasto.** Limited in early works; some later works mix thick

- **Order of work.** Ground (bought), then underdrawing, then a "very thin
  underpainting," then paint; small details were added last,
  over finished passages.

## 7. Condition and aging

- **Fragility.** The thin paint made the paintings "exceptionally prone to
  damage"; many micro-losses come from abrasion in past
  cleaning.
- **Smalt discoloration.** Smalt has partly lost its color in one painting:
  low potassium (4.9 wt%) and changed cobalt coordination show an
  intermediate stage of degradation; a simulation of the original colors
  comes out cooler and bluer. Smalt can turn brown over
  time.
- **Craquelure.** One painting has an elongated craquelure, probably from
  pressure on the back.
- **Pentimenti.** Few.

## 8. Greens

- **Mostly mixed.** The Dresden team (14 paintings) writes that "the
  palette was very sparing" but the greens show a "lush variety"
  ("üppige Vielfalt"). The true greens were "copper-containing pigments
  and green earth." Greens were often mixed from blue and yellow: Prussian
  blue "very often," smalt and cobalt blue as well, with yellow ocher,

## 4. Canvas and ground

**Thread counts (plain weave unless noted).** These are measurements of individual paintings, not period averages.

| Canvas | Threads/cm | Tag |
| --- | --- | --- |
| French 18th-century hemp | mostly 12–14 × 9.5–13 | [V] |
| French 18th century, hemp warp and linen weft | 17 × 14 | [V] |
| French 19th century | 10 × 6 (coarse) to 16 × 10 | [V] |
| Twill linen, 1830 | 30 × 29 | [V] |
| Fine linen, 1855 | 38 × 34 | [V] |
| Commercial canvas, 1879/80 | 26.0 × 29.9 | [V] |
| Commercial roll (Tasset et L'Hôte), 1888–90 | ~12 × 15–17 (e.g., 12.3 × 17.3) | [S] |

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].

- **Expect a trace.** Even a good lift leaves a tint, streaks along the
  wipe or a rim where it stopped. Look at a detail crop before you call it
  clean, and before you paint over it. Thick paint takes many fresh, dipped
  wipes.
- **One lift, then a new plan.** If the same passage needs lifting twice,
  change what goes on it before painting it again.

## Time

- Time passes only as you paint or `wait`. Paint dries on its own clock:
  lead white and umber fast, lakes and vermilion slow, thin paint faster than
  thick. Added medium and the slower oils (walnut, poppy) slow it; an
  absorbent ground sets thin paint laid straight on it quickly.
- **Check `drying(x, y)` at several points** along the next pass, its edges
  included: thick and thin parts of one passage dry at different rates.
- A painting can take months of painted time. Let layers dry between
  campaigns; that is what lets the next one sit on top.

## Finishing

- An unvarnished picture keeps its matte and glossy passages as painted.
  A varnish (where the easel has one) makes it all glossy: darks deepen.

## 9. The tubes here

The supplied box contains lead white, smalt, pale smalt, yellow ochre,
red earth, vermilion, raw umber, bone black, cobalt blue, chrome yellow,
Prussian blue, green earth, Rinmann's green, copper green, Naples yellow
and rose madder: a selection
from materials documented across Friedrich's career. Ochers and yellow
earths correspond to yellow ochre; red earths and red iron oxide to red
earth; cinnabar to vermilion. The supplied copper green is verdigris
ground in oil.

Naples yellow is lead antimonate. The supplied red lake is rose madder,
a madder lake on alumina. The easel guide lists each tube's
properties.

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with layered grounds laid from the tubes.
  Knife application levels the weave; roller and brush application leave
  their own fine texture. The preparation is dry when painting starts.
- **Drawing.** Graphite pencils, black chalk and ruled lines.
- **Paint.** Tube mixtures can be ground in linseed, walnut or poppy oil.
  Added oil makes a mixture more transparent and fluid. `turps=` thins it
  with solvent that evaporates as the paint is laid; `thinner=` leaves
  solvent in the film to evaporate over painting time. The guide describes
  both methods.
- **Taking paint off.** Brushes pick up wet paint as they pass. A rag
  wipes or blots wet paint; a painting knife scrapes it with its blade.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

The reference library seems like a valuable resource for in-depth information. Will use the `reference` command to search for relevant information or `reference_list` to browse the titles to better understand how to approach the task.


Considering a subject in the style of Caspar David Friedrich, aiming for a compelling oil painting simulation, focusing on sublime northern landscapes is the initial direction. The key elements appear to be twilight, strong spatial contrast, and a luminous atmosphere. The goal is to identify a specific, original scene within this framework.


Focusing on the sky, a deeply graded twilight seems crucial, transitioning from warm hues at the horizon to cooler blues above. Considering the foreground, a silhouetted, craggy rock formation will provide the necessary contrast against the luminous sky, and mist-veiled distant landforms will add depth. This combination should capture the desired sublime northern landscape aesthetic.


Analyzing specific elements: the rocky crag offers visual complexity and textural contrast to balance the sky. The solitary tree, whether oak or pine, will establish a strong vertical element, acting as a bridge between the foreground and the heavens, contrasting the landscape. The contemplative figure or small boat at the water's edge will add a human scale to the vastness.

- An **oil ground** (the default) absorbs nothing: paint stays open and
  glossy longer. An **absorbent ground** (`absorbent=true`) drinks the oil of
  thin paint: matte, lean, quick to set, colors that sit on the surface;
  thick paint is barely touched. Choose before you start: it is the
  canvas's character.
- A **toned ground** (a little ochre, umber or black in the white) sets the
  middle value from the first stroke; a white ground keeps everything high
  in key and lets thin paint glow.
"}

ecies are largely free of suckers and epicormic growth, unlike the hybrid common lime. Open-grown trees are dense and round, and become as wide as tall.
- **Twigs and buds.** "Slender, zigzag, green-brown or red-tinged (particularly in the winter)." The terminal bud is false; buds are plump with one side bulging.
- **Bark.** Gray or brown, with shallow furrows and flat ridges. "Numerous burls and sprouts often found around the base".
- **Old limes.** They live over 1000 years even when coppiced. Very old stools may have lost their heartwood to rot. Limes were coppiced for long straight poles and can be pollarded.

### 3.5 Oak (*Quercus robur*, pedunculate; *Q. petraea*, sessile)

- **Habit.** In *Q. robur* the main trunk "tends to disappear in the crown, developing irregular boughs with twisting branches." *Q. petraea* usually keeps a main stem with boughs that gradually decrease in size. Heights are usually about 30 m, with diameters up to 1 m. Individuals can live over 1000 years and reach 3–4 m in diameter. The crown is round.
- **Twigs and buds.** Twigs are moderate in thickness and yellow-brown. Buds are "angled, short and round". **General knowledge:** oak buds cluster at the shoot tip, so several shoots start from one point, which gives oak its crooked, clustered branching.
- **Twig shedding (cladoptosis).** In cladoptosis an abscission layer forms and the twig "is shed cleanly," as leaves are. In oak, most shed twigs are one year old and leafless."}

- **Needles.** In pairs, twisted.

### 3.7 Norway spruce (*Picea abies*)

- **Habit.** A straight, regular trunk up to 50–60 m, usually living 200–300 years. "The crown is regularly conic, columnar, with whorled, short and stout branches, the upper level ascending and the lower drooping". Free-standing trees keep green branches down to the ground. Branches are inclined to hanging, as an adaptation to snow load.
- **Branching types.** Young spruces branch in flat "plates" up to about 20 years. After that they develop either the *Plattenfichte* type, with horizontal second-order branches, or the *Kammfichte* ("comb spruce") type, whose second- and higher-order branches hang down like a fringe. A third type is the *Bürstenfichte* ("brush spruce"). Comb spruces dominate on well-supplied sites. Plate spruces dominate on poor bogs and at extreme altitudes.
- **Bark.** Orange-brown. Red-brown and scaly, later gray with flaking scales or plates. Drops of resin are common on trunk and branches.

### 3.8 Willow (white willow, *Salix alba*; other tree willows)

- **The tree.** A fast-growing tree of riverbanks and floodplains, very tolerant of flooding. It "can readily reproduce from suckers or from adventitious roots". The bark is dark gray and deeply fissured with corky ridges. The narrow leaves are silver-gray, and white willow is "cultivated as osiers, characterised by having pliable branches". Medium-lived.
"}

{"id": "oil-glazes", "title": "Glazing and scumbling at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Glazing and scumbling (over dry paint)

- **Glaze**: a transparent paint (lakes, viridian, ultramarine, a little of
  anything) with plenty of medium (0.7 to 0.85), `hand="glaze"`, over a dry
  passage. It deepens and saturates and lets the light underneath through;
  it rescues a chalky passage. Over impasto it pools in the valleys and
  thins on the ridges, which then shine through. Too much pigment, or any
  white, lays an opaque veil: try it small first. A glaze over the whole
  picture to pull it together has failed more often than it has worked.
- **Scumble**: light paint dragged thin over a dry darker passage, broken
  by the surface. A light load and
  `hand="scumble"` often lay opaque dabs. The veils that blended in came
  from paint thinned with `thinner`, laid in several light passes. Try it
  on the scratch canvas first.
- Glazes and scumbles want the passage under them **dry** (`wait` until
  `drying` says so): over open paint they just mix.
"}

{"id": "oil-blending", "title": "Blending at the easel", "page": 1, "pages": 1, "next_page": null, "text": "## Blending

- **Blend inside one passage.** Shape the mask like the passage, with its
  edge where the paint already matches. Keep everything you want to keep
  outside the mask, dry shapes included: the blender carries wet paint onto
  them.
- **Look after each pass.** The blender lifts paint as it moves it. When
  darks go pale, texture flattens or the weave shows through, stop.
- **A seam that keeps coming back** needs another method. A smaller patch
  blended again rebuilds the box. Try something else across the whole
  transition on the scratch canvas: a thin tint of the original recipe,
  interlocking strokes of the two neighboring colors over dry paint, or the
  connected passage repainted up to its natural edges.
"}

e, from the above:* snow sits as a ridge along the upper side of limbs that are near horizontal and thick enough to stop bounce. Forks and crotches collect it. Steep limbs and thin, springy twigs hold little except in wet snow near 0 °C, which can bridge between twigs.
- **What falls off, and when.** Snow slides off branches "if the branches provide an unstable or slanting support." Loads balanced on branch ends bend them into steep slopes, which then release. Slight warming melts snow first at "the points of attachment to their supports," so masses slide off before they melt away. Wind shakes crowns, and deciduous trees lose snow mostly to that shaking, not to direct wind.
- **Hoarfrost and rime (DWD definitions).** *Raureif* (hoarfrost) is "mostly thin, only loosely attached and fragile ice needles or scales," formed almost entirely by deposition from vapor. It needs humidity around 90% or more, weak wind and usually temperatures below −8 °C. Its crystals are like snowflakes under a lens, often needle-shaped. *Raueis* (rime) is a granular, "very firmly attached" deposit of supercooled fog droplets, milky white from trapped air. It forms mainly in fog at −2 to −10 °C, and strong wind favors it. Its "ice flags" point into the wind. *Klareis* (clear ice) forms at 0 to −3 °C. Fog-frost deposits "show their typical growth against the wind," mostly on near-vertical surfaces, and can grow into heavy loads. Deposits on tree branches often fall to the ground below.
"}

events.text:
Beginning the design process, aiming for a painting evocative of Caspar David Friedrich. Considering how to translate his characteristic mood and style using available resources and techniques. The primary focus will be on faithfully capturing the essence of his work within the system's capabilities.


Considering canvas proportions; Friedrich favored horizontal formats, around 4:3 or 1.35:1. A width of 1000 pixels with a height of 750 pixels offers a clean 4:3 ratio. Initial research suggests Friedrich used fine linen with a reddish-ochre ground layer applied to level the weave.


The initial ground layer will be a reddish-ochre tone. A warm yellowish-brown intermediate layer follows, with a light pearl-gray/whitish top ground completing the preparation. The horizon line will be positioned low, approximately two-thirds down the canvas, to emphasize the sky.


Analyzing how to construct the twilight sky. The horizon will feature warm, luminous colors transitioning upwards through cooler tones to a deep zenith. Careful blending and stippling are essential to avoid unintended muddy colors. The rising moon will be positioned within the right-center sky, providing balance.


Considering how to structure the scene's foreground and mid-ground elements. The great oak and moon need careful placement; the oak on the left will create a strong vertical element. The moon should be positioned to highlight its light through the cloud banks.

Analyzing the distant headlands; a two-tiered arrangement will add depth. The farther ridge needs a cooler, lighter tone to emphasize its distance. A closer headland with a deeper color will frame the water channel.


Considering the water's reflection of the twilight sky, horizontal bands of color will be employed. Warm amber-rose tones near the horizon will transition to deeper blues and greens in the mid-ground. A subtle path of moon shimmer will be positioned directly below the moon, with the inclusion of two distant sailboats.


Considering the shoreline, the crag will be formed with angular planes in shades of gray-blue and earth tones, referencing the geological descriptions. Darker shadow faces will be used to emphasize fissures and crevices, with moss and lichen in damp areas.

The monumental ancient oak will be rendered with a wide, deeply fissured trunk. The trunk will disappear into the crown, then divide into heavy, twisting primary boughs.


Considering the oak's structure: a stag-horn bough will be central-right, rising towards the sky, with twisted limbs spreading outward. The foliage will be sparse, autumn-winter, with remaining leaves in russet-bronze and dark olive-umber.

I need to place a solitary figure on a flat-topped boulder, positioned in profile or three-quarters from behind, gazing at the moon. The figure's dark clothing will be a blend of dark green-black tones. A weathered wooden object will be leaned beside the boulders on the left.


The composition's left flank requires a focal point; a wayside cross or monolith will serve as an anchor. The entire composition must be validated against the studio rules, specifically ensuring no mirrored coordinates and independent shape creation.

Campaign 1 focuses on canvas preparation and graphite underdrawing.
